entities.summary:
Albert Herrmann (1886-1945) was a prominent German archaeologist and geographer whose scholarly contributions significantly advanced geographic knowledge and cartographic accuracy during the modern era. Born in Hanover, Herrmann dedicated his career to bridging gaps in geographic understanding during a period marked by imperial expansion and the imperatives of accurate mapping.

Herrmann's academic specialization encompassed the geography of the ancient Mediterranean world, a region of enduring historical significance, and Chinese geography, reflecting the cosmopolitan scope of his research interests. His work with ancient Mediterranean geography contributed to improved cartographic accuracy and enhanced scholarly understanding of classical civilizations and their spatial dimensions. Concurrently, his expertise in Chinese geography reflected broader intellectual currents of the early twentieth century, where European scholars increasingly engaged with non-Western geographic traditions and knowledge systems.

Beyond traditional archaeological and geographic scholarship, Herrmann gained recognition for his theoretical works examining the historical location and nature of Atlantis. These investigations, while speculative in nature, demonstrated his willingness to engage with interdisciplinary questions that bridged mythology, geography, and historical interpretation. His cartographic work positioned him within the broader field of cartographers, contributing to the systematic improvement of maps and geographic representation during a transformative period.

Active throughout the Modern era, Herrmann's intellectual legacy encompassed both the advancement of geographic knowledge and contributions to the foundations of contemporary global order. His passing in 1945 marked the conclusion of a scholarly career that spanned periods of unprecedented geographic, political, and technological transformation.
